principle: International organizations can possess international legal personality distinct from member states.
practice_note: Claims capacity, treaty capacity, privileges and immunities, responsibility.

principle: Organizations may possess powers necessary to perform their functions even when not textually explicit.
Organizations derive authority from treaties or founding instruments.
leading_authority_or_example: UN Charter; WHO Constitution; WTO Agreement; IMF Articles
practice_note: Mandate analysis begins with text, object, purpose, and institutional practice.

principle: Member states delegate powers through treaties, decisions, or institutional practice.
practice_note: Authority varies by organization and field.

principle: Some bodies issue decisions binding on members under their constituent instruments.
leading_authority_or_example: Security Council Chapter VII; WTO dispute settlement
practice_note: Binding force must be traced to a legal source.

principle: Organizations generate non-binding standards, guidelines, recommendations, and technical norms.
leading_authority_or_example: WHO guidance; ILO recommendations; OECD standards
practice_note: Soft law may shape conduct even without formal binding status.

principle: Expert bodies influence law through knowledge, metrics, classifications, and standards.
practice_note: Authority can be epistemic as well as legal.

principle: Institutions and officials may hold immunities necessary for independent function.
practice_note: Immunity must be connected to function and accountability concerns.

principle: International organizations can bear responsibility for internationally wrongful acts.
leading_authority_or_example: ILC Draft Articles on Responsibility of International Organizations
practice_note: Attribution, breach, aid/assistance, and member-state responsibility must be analyzed carefully.
